profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional academic hospital's women's services team is planning a pilot pathway for second-trimester pregnancy termination referrals, using evidence that dilatation and evacuation (D&E) can be performed safely by skilled physicians in selected ambulatory settings rather than routing nearly all such cases to the main hospital OR. The meeting is a planning session, not a clinical debate: the agenda is to define the pilot's operational frame for second-trimester D&E referrals, decide what provider background and site requirements should be written into the draft pathway, determine how anesthesia involvement will be represented, assign ownership for the eligibility checklist and workflow map, and set a timeline for a quality committee submission. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for a draft protocol, staffing assumptions, and implementation steps for a pilot program.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Maternal-Fetal Medicine attending and clinical pathway lead
members.expertise: Complex pregnancy care, procedural risk stratification, referral pathway design, quality committee presentations
members.background: An obstetrician-gynecologist who trained at a high-volume academic center where second-trimester D&E was commonly performed in a hospital-affiliated outpatient procedural unit with rapid access to hospital resources when needed.
members.private_state: She wants a pilot that can be approved quickly and quietly reduce main OR congestion, and she is deliberately framing the plan in conservative language so it will seem operationally modest while still allowing a meaningful number of referrals to move out of the OR.
hidden_assumptions: If a physician has strong suction-curettage skills and prior supervised D&E exposure, that person has the appropriate clinical background for an initial pilot even if local privileging paperwork is still catching up.
Calling a site 'ambulatory' naturally includes a hospital outpatient procedure unit on the medical campus as long as transfer and backup are nearby.
When people say 'second-trimester D&E referrals' in pathway work, they are usually talking about the routine middle band of cases rather than every possible gestational age from 13 weeks onward.
Saying anesthesia will review candidates can reasonably mean chart-based screening before launch, with in-person evaluation reserved for patients who trigger concerns.

members.name: Karen Liu, RN, MSN
members.role: Perioperative nurse manager for women's procedural services
members.expertise: Ambulatory procedure operations, accreditation readiness, perioperative staffing models, transfer and recovery protocols
members.background: A nurse leader who previously managed a freestanding ambulatory surgery center and now oversees operational readiness and workflow standardization across the hospital's women's procedural areas.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid endorsing a pathway that later fails operational or regulatory review, and she is listening for wording that can be translated into existing standards without creating exceptions nursing leadership would have to defend.
hidden_assumptions: If a planning document says providers must have the appropriate clinical background, that normally presumes they are already institutionally cleared to perform those cases in that setting.

In operational discussions, 'ambulatory setting' points to a formally designated ambulatory surgery environment with defined recovery staffing, equipment standards, and licensure expectations rather than any outpatient area.
A pathway described as covering second-trimester D&E referrals should be built broadly enough to handle all referrals from 13 weeks onward unless an upper boundary is explicitly written in.
If anesthesia is said to review patients, that implies the standard perioperative workflow of formal pre-op assessment and day-of-case anesthesia coverage expectations.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the pilot should start only with providers who have the appropriate clinical background.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means gynecologists with strong suction-curettage competence and prior supervised D&E experience, even if they are only now being incorporated into the local second-trimester pathway.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means clinicians whose training is already reflected in site-specific privileging and operational clearance for those cases in the intended setting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds more polished and less legalistic than 'privileged,' so each hears it as safely conservative and assumes the other is using the same commonsense meaning from their own domain.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse moving selected second-trimester D&E cases into an ambulatory setting rather than defaulting to the main hospital OR.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the hospital's outpatient procedure unit on campus, with nearby transfer access and hospital backup if needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a formally designated ambulatory surgery environment with specific licensure, recovery staffing, and emergency-readiness standards.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Ambulatory is a common umbrella term in clinical operations, and because both options are outpatient-adjacent and sound equally safety-oriented, the regulatory distinction remains comfortably implicit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss building the pilot around second-trimester D&E referrals and women at 13 weeks or later.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the draft pathway is really for the routine referrals they are trying to reroute first, roughly the common mid-second-trimester cases that most affect OR access.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the workflow should cover the full referral category of second-trimester D&E from 13 weeks onward unless the document explicitly states a cutoff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using ordinary clinical shorthand rather than a formal inclusion table, and because no one is yet discussing edge-case patients, each person treats their boundary as the obvious default.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree anesthesia should review ambulatory candidates before the pilot goes live.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes anesthesia review can be an asynchronous chart-screening step for eligibility, with direct consultation only for selected higher-risk patients.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes review means the standard perioperative process of scheduled pre-op anesthesia evaluation and day-of-procedure staffing alignment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both versions are routinely described as anesthesia review in hospital conversation, so the phrase feels concrete enough to move planning forward without prompting either person to unpack the workflow details.
